stories.headline: Kimberly Guilfoyle resigns as ambassador to Greece amid misconduct allegations

claims.text: White House press secretary Katie Zacharia told reporters Tuesday that the administration had asked Ambassador Kimberly Guilfoyle to resign.
Guilfoyle posted her resignation on X about two hours after the administration asked her to resign.
Since late September, The Wall Street Journal has reported a series of allegations against Guilfoyle.
The Wall Street Journal reported that Guilfoyle threatened a host-country official.
The Wall Street Journal reported that Guilfoyle accepted improper gifts and services.
The Wall Street Journal reported that Guilfoyle promoted the business interests of a Greek construction and energy company.
The Wall Street Journal reported that Guilfoyle let a lobbyist for a Greek construction and energy company into private diplomatic meetings.
The Wall Street Journal reported that Guilfoyle asked a Trump donor to pay a $100,000 credit card bill in exchange for promised access to administration officials.
The British tabloid Daily Mail separately reported that Guilfoyle had alienated staff at the U.S. Embassy in Athens.
Guilfoyle denied all allegations.
Guilfoyle said she would 'vigorously defend' her name, reputation and integrity.
Guilfoyle's lawyers, David Schwartz and Jesse Binnall, said the disputed payment was for prior speaking engagements.
Guilfoyle's lawyers said her private-plane travel followed State Department guidance.
President Trump said he had not personally spoken with Guilfoyle before her resignation.
President Trump said 'I didn't like what I read' regarding the reports about Guilfoyle.
The AP, citing a senior U.S. official, reported that Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio were 'extremely pissed off' about the reports.
Rubio, speaking in Athens last week, declined to confirm or deny the allegations.
Rubio criticized reporters for treating sourced reports as 'gospel.'
A second U.S. official said the State Department's inspector general's office was reviewing the allegations.
It was unclear whether a formal investigation had been opened into the allegations against Guilfoyle.

facts: White House press secretary Katie Zacharia told reporters Tuesday that the administration had asked Ambassador Kimberly Guilfoyle to resign; Guilfoyle posted her resignation on X about two hours later.

Since late September, The Wall Street Journal has reported a series of allegations against Guilfoyle, including that she threatened a host-country official, accepted improper gifts and services, promoted the business interests of a Greek construction and energy company, let its lobbyist into private diplomatic meetings, and asked a Trump donor to pay a $100,000 credit card bill in exchange for promised access to administration officials.
The British tabloid Daily Mail separately reported that Guilfoyle had alienated staff at the U.S. Embassy in Athens.

Guilfoyle denied all allegations and said she would 'vigorously defend' her name, reputation and integrity; her lawyers, David Schwartz and Jesse Binnall, said the disputed payment was for prior speaking engagements and that her private-plane travel followed State Department guidance.

President Trump said he had not personally spoken with Guilfoyle before her resignation and said 'I didn't like what I read'; the AP, citing a senior U.S. official, reported that Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio were 'extremely pissed off' about the reports.
Rubio, speaking in Athens last week, declined to confirm or deny the allegations and criticized reporters for treating sourced reports as 'gospel.'
A second U.S. official said the State Department's inspector general's office was reviewing the allegations, though it was unclear whether a formal investigation had been opened.

House Foreign Affairs ranking member Rep. Gregory Meeks, Senate Foreign Relations ranking member Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, and House Oversight ranking member Rep. Robert Garcia, all Democrats, called for an investigation into Guilfoyle's conduct.
ladder.analysis: Guilfoyle, a former Fox News host and California prosecutor once married to Gavin Newsom and later engaged to Donald Trump Jr., was serving as Trump's ambassador to Greece, a post of growing strategic importance given Greece's role in energy transit and Eastern Mediterranean security. Her departure follows weeks of reporting on alleged financial and ethical improprieties, capped by the administration itself requesting her resignation rather than her stepping down unprompted. The episode also surfaces a broader structural trend noted by a former State Department union head: the share of U.S. ambassadors who are career Foreign Service officers has fallen from roughly 60% historically to about 5% under Trump, with most posts now going to political allies, donors or supporters rather than career diplomats.
ladder.steelman: Across the reporting, the throughline isn't partisan but structural: a political appointee with no diplomatic background faced detailed, documented allegations of blending personal financial interests with an ambassadorship, prompting even her own administration to seek her removal rather than defend her — a case study in the risks of the sharp rise in non-career ambassadorial appointments.
ladder.implications: The State Department inspector general's review, if formalized, could determine whether Guilfoyle faces further consequences, while Democrats' calls for investigation may keep the matter alive in congressional oversight.

claims.text: Top Republicans have privately conceded that House control is 'all but gone.'
GOP-aligned groups work to limit their losses.
The Democratic-aligned Senate Majority PAC is scaling back ad spending in the Georgia and North Carolina Senate races.

Democrats have pulled back ad spending in a red-leaning Arizona House district.

facts: Politico reports that top Republicans have privately conceded that House control is "all but gone," even as GOP-aligned groups work to limit their losses.

The Democratic-aligned Senate Majority PAC is scaling back ad spending in the Georgia and North Carolina Senate races as Republican spending there slows, with Sen. Jon Ossoff (GA) and former Gov. Roy Cooper (NC) increasingly seen as favored.
The GOP's Senate Leadership Fund has increased spending for Sen. Pete Ricketts in Nebraska after previously boosting spending in Kansas and South Carolina.

The Congressional Leadership Fund, a House GOP leadership-aligned PAC, is redirecting money away from purple-district incumbents Rep. Tom Kean (NJ) and Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks (IA) toward GOP incumbents in more Trump-favorable districts, including Reps. Monica De La Cruz (TX) and Rob Wittman (VA).
Democrats have pulled back ad spending in a red-leaning Arizona House district, while Republicans continue heavy spending to try to flip the Maine seat being vacated by Rep. Jared Golden.

The Guardian identifies competitive Senate races in New Hampshire (John Sununu vs. Chris Pappas), Kansas (Roger Marshall vs. Adam Hamilton), and Minnesota (Michele Tafoya vs. Peggy Flanagan), along with House races in Florida's 13th, Wisconsin's 1st, Alabama's 2nd, New Mexico's 2nd, Texas's 34th, and New Jersey's 7th districts, plus the Nevada governor's race (Joe Lombardo vs. Aaron Ford).
Cook Political Report rates the New Hampshire Senate race a tossup.
ladder.analysis: The reporting centers on where the two parties are choosing to spend money in the run-up to the midterms. The pattern described here — Democratic money retreating from Georgia and North Carolina as those Senate races tilt toward Democratic candidates, and House GOP money shifting from suburban "purple" districts to safer Trump-won turf — is consistent with Politico's report that senior Republicans no longer expect to hold the House. At the same time, The Guardian's list of lower-profile Senate, House, and gubernatorial races shows that both parties still see a meaningful number of contests as competitive, meaning the overall midterm picture is not settled even if the macro trend favors Democrats.
ladder.steelman: The reporting shows campaign money flowing out of races seen as decided and into a narrower set of contests, including some, like Kansas or Alabama's 2nd district, where the traditional partisan lean doesn't match the apparent competitiveness described by The Guardian.

stories.headline: Supreme Court will review dispute over records from Elon Musk's DOGE

claims.text: The Supreme Court agreed Tuesday to review a dispute over records from Elon Musk's Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE), as well as a separate asylum case.
The watchdog group Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington (CREW) sued DOGE under the Freedom of Information Act seeking access to its records.
Lower courts ordered DOGE to disclose certain materials, including administrator directives to employees, any plans to access classified information, and a deposition from DOGE's head, Amy Gleason.
The Trump administration argues DOGE is a 'presidential advisory body' that only makes recommendations and should be shielded from FOIA, citing separation-of-powers concerns.
In an earlier stage of this case last year, the Supreme Court sided with DOGE and narrowed the scope of required disclosures.
In that earlier stage, the three liberal justices dissented.
CREW later withdrew some of its requests.

The second case involves Izuchukwu Ozurumba, a Nigerian national denied asylum after a judge found he provided 'material support' to a terrorist group called the Unknown Gunmen by cooking meals for its members for six months.
Ozurumba was deported to Nigeria in 2025.
The 4th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals had ruled his conduct did not meet the 'material' support threshold.
The Supreme Court is expected to issue decisions in both cases by next summer.
According to the administration, the asylum case has implications for thousands of immigration cases annually.
Both cases arrived at the Supreme Court amid the Trump administration's broader efforts to limit the federal bureaucracy and tighten immigration enforcement.
Both cases continue a pattern of the Court taking up multiple significant immigration-related disputes this term.

ladder.analysis: The DOGE case centers on a core legal question: whether an entity the Trump administration describes as a 'presidential advisory body' tasked with providing recommendations functions instead as a government agency subject to transparency laws, or whether it is properly shielded as an internal advisory arm of the White House. The outcome could shape how future presidential initiatives that wield significant practical power—without formal agency status—are treated under federal transparency law. The asylum case, meanwhile, asks how broadly the law's 'material support' bar for terrorism should be read, with implications for thousands of immigration cases annually according to the administration. Both cases arrived at the Supreme Court amid the Trump administration's broader efforts to limit the federal bureaucracy and tighten immigration enforcement, and both also continue a pattern of the Court taking up multiple significant immigration-related disputes this term.
ladder.steelman: Both cases turn on the same underlying tension the Court will have to resolve: how to draw lines—between executive advice and executive action in the DOGE case, and between incidental and material assistance in the terrorism-support case—when the law's text leaves room for competing, good-faith interpretations on both sides.
ladder.implications: The Court's rulings, expected by next summer, could set precedents affecting how transparency laws apply to future presidential initiatives that operate with significant practical power but ambiguous legal status, and could also redefine how broadly 'material support' for terrorism is interpreted in immigration cases nationwide.

stories.headline: Ukrainian suspect goes on trial in Germany over Nord Stream pipeline sabotage
body: A Ukrainian man, Serhii Kuznetsov, went on trial in Hamburg on Wednesday, accused of playing a leading role in the sabotage of Russia's Nord Stream gas pipelines in 2022. Prosecutors have charged him with a war crime, alleging he ordered a team of divers and an explosives expert to attack civilian infrastructure. Kuznetsov, who appeared relaxed and smiled in court, denies all charges.

Kuznetsov’s defence lawyer, Nicola Canestrini, told the BBC outside the courtroom that after four years of investigation, prosecutors had found no witnesses, forensics, DNA, or fingerprints. The defence also argued that because Kuznetsov, as a soldier, is bound to secrecy, he cannot receive a fair trial — noting that he is unable to disclose his whereabouts or potential alibi witnesses if he was on a secret operation. They further contended that his extradition was flawed because the war crime allegation was not mentioned at the time of his arrest.

The Nord Stream pipelines — three of four gas lines — were destroyed by explosives on 26 September 2022 in the Baltic Sea off the Danish island of Bornholm. German investigators later focused on a yacht called the Andromeda, rented from the port of Rostock, and said they found traces of subsea explosives aboard. Kuznetsov was arrested in August 2025 at a hotel near Rimini, Italy, under a European arrest warrant, and extradited to Germany late last year.

In their indictment, German prosecutors allege the sabotage plot was conceived 'acting by order of Ukrainian state agencies.' Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has consistently denied any involvement. Oleksandr Merezhko, chair of the Ukrainian parliament’s Foreign Affairs Committee, called the German account 'one of the versions,' adding that Nord Stream 2 was 'nothing but a tool used by Russia' to prepare for war.

The trial is diplomatically sensitive because Germany is one of Ukraine’s closest allies. Stefan Meister of the German Council on Foreign Relations said successive chancellors tried to depoliticise the case by leaving it to the judiciary. A second Ukrainian suspect, Volodymyr Zhuravlov, is also wanted in connection with the sabotage; Croatia approved his extradition last month, though the timing remains unclear. The Hamburg trial continues.

stories.headline: Pakistan imposes emergency rule in Imran Khan's stronghold
body: Pakistan has declared a state of emergency in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, the northwestern province governed by imprisoned former Prime Minister Imran Khan's party, deploying the army, closing schools, and partially shutting down the internet. The federal government suspended the provincial administration, citing constitutional authority to protect the population from terrorism, as thousands of Khan's supporters marched through the province demanding his release.

Federal Information Minister Attah Tarrar told journalists Sunday that the PTI-led provincial government was "hand in glove with the terrorists," though he did not provide evidence and had not offered further details as of Tuesday. Schools in Peshawar and most areas had reopened, and internet services were restored by then. Police would not confirm detentions, but most PTI leaders in the province have gone into hiding; dozens of supporters protested Tuesday in Bara, Khyber district, where tear gas was reportedly used.

The whereabouts of provincial Chief Minister Sohail Afridi, a PTI member who led the recent march, remain unknown. His party claims he has been arrested; the government says he is in protective custody. The crackdown comes amid a broader effort to suppress dissent: three of Khan's sisters were arrested in September and remain detained, accused of mobilizing supporters. Khan himself has been imprisoned since August 2023 on multiple corruption convictions he says are politically motivated, and his health has been a growing concern.

Analysts questioned the government's justification for emergency rule. "I do not see the link with terrorism," said journalist and commentator Arifa Noor. Farzana Sheikh, associate fellow at Chatham House, called the timing "disingenuous." Michael Kugelman of the Atlantic Council noted growing restlessness among PTI supporters over Khan's health, suggesting the move aims to "send a very strong message" and make it harder for the party to pressure the government. Tarar insisted there was "no political agenda" and pointed to pre-decision talks.

Observers pointed to the military's heavy influence. Defense analyst Zahid Hussain said, "The balance of power is completely shifted to the military establishment." Sheikh argued the military feels emboldened by its perceived good relations with the White House and regional role. Yet Pakistan faces multiple challenges: rising militancy (it ranked first on the Global Terrorism Index 2026), tensions with Afghanistan and India, and commitments to Saudi Arabia. Several experts warned the emergency could backfire, increasing instability and anger. "It is reckless, given the multiple challenges the country is facing," Hussain said, adding that similar powers could be used elsewhere. Noor described the standoff as "a train crash" that both sides see coming but cannot stop.

stories.headline: Iran steps up Hormuz surveillance; ship sinks after striking mine in Strait of Hormuz
stories.byline: International & World desk · anchored on AP
body: Iran’s military said it has expanded its surveillance of the Strait of Hormuz by deploying new units to target ships, as attacks in the waterway surged and oil transit fell sharply. The navy said the units would maintain “real time surveillance of enemy activities and maritime traffic in the region,” warned vessels not to switch off their transponders, and urged them to coordinate with Iranian armed forces for safe passage. An Iranian official told Reuters that Tehran had started using different offensive tactics against vessels it considered in violation of its restrictions about 10 days ago, adding that this had led to an increase in attacks on such ships, with one goal being to influence the outcome of the November midterm elections in the US.

On Wednesday, Iran’s Revolutionary Guard Corps navy said a cargo ship had sunk after hitting a naval mine in the Strait of Hormuz — the first time Iran has reported a ship sinking after hitting a mine during the war. State television quoted a Guard statement saying the ship was traveling on what it called an illegal and dangerous route when it hit the mine Wednesday morning. The unidentified ship, shown tilted in the water and spewing a thick plume of smoke, was carrying 2,500 containers, the broadcast said. Few details were available, including about the fate of the crew.

According to maritime tracking firm Kpler, 10 tankers were struck in the strait between September 28 and October 4, followed by another strike on October 5. The UK Maritime Trade Operations centre separately recorded 15 other attacks between October 6 and October 14, with 11 of them occurring in just the past four days. Kpler reported that only 2.9 million barrels of oil were carried through the waterway on October 11, the lowest level this month, down from nearly 20.8 million barrels on October 8. The pre-war average was 17.1 million barrels a day. Oil prices continued to climb Wednesday, with Brent crude futures gaining 89 cents to $106.58 a barrel.

Iran maintains that its attacks and restrictions in the waterway are a matter of national security and self-defence in response to the US-Israel war. In its latest report on Sunday, the US Navy-led Joint Maritime Information Center noted that the threat to merchant shipping in the Strait of Hormuz remained “severe,” the second-highest level. It said attacks by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, “attempted attacks, and/or harassment activity persisted including UAV overflight, targeted surveillance of merchant shipping, and occasional VHF hailing.” A US military official confirmed to Reuters that Iran had changed tactics, with the IRGC using unarmed spotters in small boats to identify potential targets after Washington destroyed much of Iran’s radar capabilities. The official said US forces confronted one such vessel, told its occupants to abandon ship, and then destroyed it.

US Central Command rejected assertions by the commander of the IRGC that Tehran controls the Strait of Hormuz and would sink approaching US warships, saying on X: “IRGC’s navy commander has no navy. American forces and regional partners clearly control the Strait of Hormuz.” CENTCOM added that US forces assisted Gulf partners to ship more than 19 million barrels of crude oil through the strategic chokepoint on Monday. Iran’s security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, claimed that a US shuttle system using smaller vessels to transfer oil to larger tankers was an explicit target for Tehran, and that Iran has been striking five or six participating vessels nightly for weeks. “You are smuggling, but the strait is under Iran’s control, and we manage it,” he asserted.

Chris Featherstone, a political scientist at the University of York in the United Kingdom, told Al Jazeera the increased attacks and their impact on energy flows demonstrate the fragility of the strait as a key pathway for oil exports. He noted that the strait is not under Iranian control, and that Tehran’s attacks only attempt to show that Washington does not control the waterway either. “As such, US allies will increase pressure for the Trump administration to bring more stability to the region, or show a path towards achieving greater stability,” he added.

stories.headline: Hot CPI inflation pushes stocks lower, raises Fed rate-hike bets
stories.byline: Financial & Markets desk · anchored on Reuters
body: U.S. stocks fell and Treasury yields jumped Wednesday after the September consumer price index came in hotter than expected, prompting investors to raise bets on further Federal Reserve interest-rate hikes. The broad S&P 500 was down 0.6%, the Nasdaq Composite shed 0.8%, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell about 32 points, or 0.1%. The 10-year Treasury yield rose more than 7 basis points to 5.293%, and the 30-year yield climbed over 4 basis points to 5.609%.

The Labor Department's Bureau of Labor Statistics reported that the consumer price index — a broad measure of goods and services costs — rose a seasonally adjusted 0.6% in September, putting the 12-month inflation rate at 3.7%. Economists surveyed by Dow Jones had expected a 0.6% monthly gain and a 3.6% annual rate. Stripping out volatile food and energy costs, the core CPI rose 0.3% on the month and 2.6% year over year, both slightly above the 0.2% and 2.5% economists had forecast. The annual headline rate was 3.4% in August, while the core rate was 2.4%.

Surging energy costs were again the primary driver of inflation. The energy index jumped 5.2%, with gasoline prices soaring 9.1% — accounting for about half of the headline CPI gain, according to the BLS. Over the past year, gasoline has risen 34.2% and fuel oil 74.2%. Food prices were flat on the month and up 2.5% from a year ago, while shelter prices increased 0.4% and used car and truck prices rose 0.7%. Apparel prices increased 0.3% on the month and are up 3.4% annually. The average U.S. gasoline price was $4.34 a gallon, versus $3.08 a year earlier, according to AAA, and U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude futures rose about 1% to around $95 a barrel.

Following the report, futures traders raised the probability of a rate hike at the Federal Open Market Committee's Oct. 27-28 meeting to about 54%, according to the CME Group's FedWatch tool. Odds of a rate increase before year-end rose above 96%, with a near 50-50 chance of a half-percentage-point move by December. The September CPI is the final inflation reading FOMC officials will receive before their next meeting; the BLS will release September producer price index data on Thursday. 'CPI came in hot and it wasn't just fuel prices, as core inflation ran at a 3.7% annualized pace in September and 3.2% over three years,' said Sonu Varghese, chief macro strategist at Carson Group. 'The only surprise is that investors keep getting surprised by broad-based inflation. And we've yet to see the full impact of higher diesel prices and the AI boom.'

The inflation data lands after the Fed in September approved its first interest-rate hike in more than three years, a quarter-point increase that took the benchmark funds rate to a target range of 3.75%-4%. Inflation as measured by the CPI has exceeded the Fed's 2% goal since March 2021, spiking following U.S. and Israeli strikes against Iran. While supply shocks are often viewed as temporary, Fed officials fear the longer the war continues, the greater the chance the price spike becomes embedded in expectations. Prices also face pressure from President Donald Trump's tariffs and demand tied to the artificial-intelligence build-out. Several policymakers have said the Fed need not rush another hike, but most expect one this year, and market pricing implies at least two more increases in 2027. The Fed's preferred inflation gauge — the Commerce Department's personal consumption expenditures price index for September — is due later this month.

In corporate news, Bank of America shares fell 7% after the bank reported third-quarter results that included a more than $1.2 billion federal penalty tied to allegations it failed to report over $5 billion in 'suspicious' transactions and violated anti-money laundering and sanctions laws; the fine reduced third-quarter earnings by 17 cents a share and revenue missed estimates. Morgan Stanley's stock traded nearly 2% lower. Chip stocks extended recent declines, with Micron Technology down 1%, Advanced Micro Devices down 3%, and Intel and Sandisk each losing 2%. The market's reaction suggested businesses face a higher bar during third-quarter earnings season, especially in tech, where semiconductors are expected to be the largest contributor to year-over-year earnings growth. Meanwhile, the Fed's 'beige book' survey of regional economic conditions was expected later Wednesday.

stories.headline: Bank of America shares plunge 8% on revenue miss and $1.2 billion Treasury penalty
body: Bank of America Corp. shares fell 8% in early trading Wednesday after the bank reported third-quarter revenue that missed analyst estimates and disclosed a $1.2 billion penalty from U.S. regulators over failures to report suspicious transactions. The bank posted earnings per share of 91 cents, compared with the 1.10 expected by LSEG, while revenue came in at $30.12 billion against the $30.69 billion consensus. Profit declined 17% to $6.93 billion, with the regulatory fine reducing per-share earnings by 17 cents.

The revenue miss of about $570 million was driven largely by weaker-than-expected results from Wall Street trading operations. Fixed income trading revenue fell 17% to $2.55 billion, approximately $450 million below the StreetAccount estimate, as the bank cited weakness in mortgages, municipals and credit activity amid a sharp rise in interest rates. Equities trading revenue rose 10% to $2.51 billion, but that also fell short of analysts’ forecasts by nearly $300 million. Combined bond and stock trading revenue declined 5%, contrary to CEO Brian Moynihan’s previous guidance that trading revenue would be roughly flat.

Investment banking revenue dropped 11% to $1.8 billion, roughly in line with expectations and Moynihan’s earlier guidance. Net interest income, a closely watched measure of lending profitability, rose 7.9% to $16.6 billion, slightly above the StreetAccount estimate of $16.53 billion. Wells Fargo analyst Mike Mayo described the bank's capital markets results as 'easily worst in class' for the quarter.

The $1.2 billion fine, announced Tuesday, stems from U.S. regulators’ determination that the bank failed to report billions of dollars in suspicious transactions. The penalty raised questions about risk-management controls at the second-largest U.S. bank by assets. On a conference call with analysts, JPMorgan analyst Vivek Juneja noted the sharp share decline and pressed Moynihan on earlier assurances that compliance costs would be contained. 'Clearly you've had a huge charge this morning,' Juneja said. 'It's not that you can't absorb a billion… But obviously it's a reputational and confidence issue.'

CFO Alastair Borthwick attributed the bond trading shortfall to the sharp rise in interest rates during the period, saying, 'It just happens when rates go up 85 basis points in a quarter, that tends not to be good for' credit and mortgage trading businesses. Moynihan, who took the helm in 2010 and spent years resolving mortgage-related abuses from the financial crisis, now faces renewed scrutiny over whether additional risk-management issues remain undiscovered.

The disappointing report adds a sour note to an otherwise routine bank earnings week. On Tuesday, JPMorgan Chase, Goldman Sachs, Citigroup and Wells Fargo posted mixed results, with JPMorgan missing earnings and revenue estimates for the first time in years.

stories.headline: Burnham under pressure after deleted Man City dinner records emerge
body: Andy Burnham, the Prime Minister and former mayor of Greater Manchester, is facing renewed pressure after it emerged he had two hospitality dinners with Manchester City chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak at matches in 2017 and 2018 — details that were omitted from a statement released Monday by the Greater Manchester Combined Authority (GMCA) about his meetings with the club.

The GMCA statement said Burnham had a formal meeting with Al Mubarak in October 2021 at the UK Government's Global Investment Summit, and that he met the chairman "informally in the stands" at a 2019 testimonial match for Vincent Kompany. It also said that "in his capacity as mayor, he was a guest of Manchester City at home matches on a small number of occasions," but did not specify that this referred to two hospitality dinners. A previous GMCA register of declarations, seen by the BBC, detailed a "dinner with [then-Manchester City Council leader] Richard Leese and Chair of Man City" for an Everton match in August 2017, valued at £300, and a "dinner with the Chairman at the Man City/Man Utd derby at the Etihad" in April 2018, valued at approximately £699. That register has since been deleted from the GMCA website; the BBC understands the authority's policy is to only publish entries from the current mayoral term, though its website has entries dating back to 2022 despite the current term beginning in 2024.

The controversy follows Manchester City's guilty verdict in September, when an independent commission found the club had broken Premier League financial rules over a nine-year period between 2009 and 2018 by creating "sham" contracts with commercial partners to secretly funnel more than £830m into their football operations. City denies any wrongdoing and has lodged an appeal. Sanctions have not yet been announced.

Burnham sparked widespread controversy last month when he said he would be "really concerned" if the club's owners now sold up. At Prime Minister's Questions on Wednesday, when asked whether anyone at the club had raised the charges with him or his team, Burnham said: "They did not raise those issues with me." He told MPs he was happy for "everything to be set out in full," referring to the GMCA statement as "a full statement of my key dealings with the owners of Manchester City Football Club." When asked why the statement did not refer to the two dinners, and what the difference is between "everything" and "key dealings," the PM's press secretary referred back to the GMCA statement.

Political pressure is mounting. Tory shadow sports minister Louie French said: "Andy Burnham promised the country and House of Commons full transparency on his dealings with Manchester City. This was essential after his inappropriate intervention into football." Reform UK's Robert Jenrick said "this saga stinks" as he accused Burnham of having apparently "concealed his extensive links to Man City's owners." Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has demanded that No 10 release all details of meetings between the prime minister and senior figures at the club. Downing Street has defended the two dinners, saying this was hospitality received at home games, which had been declared, rather than separate meetings with the club chairman.

stories.headline: BlackRock buys majority stake in Humana's CenterWell clinics for $2.8B
body: Humana announced Tuesday that BlackRock will acquire Welsh, Carson, Anderson & Stowe’s majority stake in CenterWell Senior Primary Care, the insurer’s network of 150 Medicare Advantage-focused clinics, in a transaction valued at $2.8 billion.

The deal marks the exit of private equity firm Welsh Carson, which made its initial investment in CenterWell more than six years ago and has poured at least $1.8 billion into the venture since 2020. BlackRock will take over as the majority owner.

Over the next two years, Humana said the transaction will help fund existing clinic operations, support the addition of new clinics, and enable other strategic acquisitions. The clinics are part of Humana’s CenterWell brand, which focuses on primary care for Medicare Advantage beneficiaries.
The move reflects a typical private equity timeline, with Welsh Carson exiting after a six-year-plus holding period.

stories.headline: FBI arrests OpenAI employee accused of planting hidden recording device in conference room
body: Federal prosecutors have charged Abdulrahman Alfozan, a Saudi national who worked on OpenAI's product team, with using an electronic device to intercept oral communications after the company discovered a hidden recording device in an executive conference room at its San Francisco office. Alfozan was fired and arrested on October 9, about a week after OpenAI found the surveillance device, and faces up to five years in prison if convicted.

According to the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Northern District of California, the device had been inserted into a USB port on the back of a television in the conference room. OpenAI said it used its internal AI models to analyze what the company described as a "sophisticated" device containing "advanced encryption, audio monitoring capabilities, and a mechanism for transferring data designed to evade monitoring," though the degree to which it is technically distinct from other recording devices remains unclear.

Prosecutors said OpenAI caught Alfozan after he was seen looking behind the television where the device was placed and where the company had positioned a camera that allegedly recorded the employee. OpenAI spokesperson Nate Evans confirmed that Alfozan joined the AI maker in July 2025 and worked on the product team.

OpenAI said it alerted the FBI after the discovery and stated: "At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data." The exact purpose of the recording device is not clear, but FBI Director Kash Patel said the alleged scheme was intended to "capture sensitive communications about the company's super intelligence technology."

"Protecting American SI innovation is essential to safeguarding our nation's economic strength and national security, and the FBI views that mission as one of our highest counterintelligence priorities," Patel said in a statement that an FBI spokesperson reiterated when reached. Neither Alfozan nor his attorney could be immediately reached for comment.

stories.headline: Google DeepMind CEO Warns AI Hacking Incidents Are 'Early Warning Shots'
stories.byline: Tech / AI desk · anchored on Reuters
body: Demis Hassabis, co-founder and chair of Google DeepMind and chief scientist at Alphabet, warned Wednesday that recent hacking incidents involving autonomous AI agents are "early warning shots" that could escalate into major security breaches within the next two years if companies and governments do not strengthen safeguards. Speaking at the International AI Summit in Dublin, Hassabis said the technology industry must improve security around increasingly capable systems, drawing lessons from safety-critical sectors such as biology and nuclear power.

"I think these (hacking incidents) are early warning shots for us that systems aren't that powerful yet, so the incidents aren't that major," Hassabis said, according to Reuters. "But they could be (major) looking into next year and the next couple years if we don't do more work as an industry, as individual companies and governments on securing these systems." He emphasized the need to "asymmetrically power the defenders" by using AI defensively to fix vulnerabilities before systems are widely released.

Hassabis called for building secure testing environments, or "sandboxes," for autonomous AI agents before deployment, and urged the creation of an international standards organization for critical-system protection. He cautioned that such a body must remain flexible, avoid suppressing innovation, and apply certification requirements proportionate to evolving technological risks. He also noted that AI is a "dual-purpose technology" that can deliver benefits such as treating diseases but can also be repurposed by bad actors, and that misalignment—ensuring AI systems adhere to their intended goals—is a key concern.

The warning comes amid broader industry calls for tighter AI safety measures. Brad Smith, president of Microsoft, argued that AI faces fewer safety requirements than everyday products like washing machines and milk, and pressed governments to establish tougher, faster-moving rules. Last month, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei urged the AI industry to deliberately slow model development, warning that unchecked advances could create catastrophic risks within months. Nikesh Arora, CEO of Palo Alto Networks, cautioned that AI could accelerate vulnerability discovery while many companies remain years behind in cybersecurity modernization, predicting major breaches in the coming years.

Hassabis, a Nobel Prize laureate in chemistry for developing an AI model that predicts protein structures, struck an optimistic tone about AI's potential to advance science, particularly in mathematics and biology. However, he stressed that AI systems still require real-world testing loops—hypothesis, experiment, data gathering, and validation—and that mathematicians' skills are increasingly needed for AI safety. "From others, other sectors that have dealt with safety-critical systems, whether it's biology or nuclear, I think there are a lot of lessons that can be learned about containment systems," he said. "I think we need to start taking that seriously, bring experts in from those areas."
